title: Eisenhower's Note in Case of Failure
text:
On June 5, 1944, General Dwight D. Eisenhower had already given the order for the Allied invasion of Normandy, after postponing it once because of bad weather. Thousands of ships and aircraft were moving. Nothing more could be changed, and no one knew whether the landings would succeed.

That day he wrote a short note in pencil, to be released if the invasion failed. It said that the landings had failed to gain a satisfactory foothold and that he had withdrawn the troops. It said his decision to attack at that time and place had been based on the best information available, and that the soldiers, airmen and sailors had done all that bravery and devotion to duty could do. It ended: "If any blame or fault attaches to the attempt it is mine alone."

In the draft he first wrote that the troops "have been withdrawn", then crossed it out and wrote "I have withdrawn" instead. He also misdated the note July 5.

The landings succeeded, and the note was never needed. He later gave it to his naval aide, Harry Butcher, and it is now kept at the Eisenhower Presidential Library.
lesson: Before you know how a decision turns out, be ready to own it completely. Credit can be shared; responsibility should not be.
source: Eisenhower's handwritten note, Eisenhower Presidential Library, Abilene, Kansas
